articles.title: Listening before legislating
articles.content: EVERY World Mental Health Day arrives with a theme, a hashtag, and a flurry of panels. This year’s call to centre the voices of people with lived experience deserves more than a single day. It requires an honest accounting of whose voices have shaped our mental health agenda, and whose have been absent from it. In clinical practice, one learns that people rarely describe their distress in the language of diagnosis. Recent events shape, and at times fortify, age-old dogmas. A young woman laments that recent allegations of sexual assault on a university campus have reinforced the view for her parents that places of learning are not safe for girls and that she must rethink her dreams. A teenage boy says he has not cried since he was nine, because he learned early what crying would cost him. A man in his 40s says he cannot tell his family he has stopped sleeping, because the word ‘depression’ would be heard as weakness, or worse, as madness. None of them is describing a disorder alone. Each is describing a world, and a mind adapting to it. Mental health does not reside only within individuals. It is shaped by homes, classrooms, workplaces, streets, and the narratives a society sustains about who may be safe, who may be vulnerable, and who may speak. Pakistan ranks near the bottom of global gender parity indices; millions of girls remain out of school. When women fear pursuing an education, or when their aspirations are quietly renegotiated, the consequences extend well beyond the economic. They appear as hopelessness, chronic anxiety, and a constriction of possibility. Boys raised to equate emotion with weakness and dominance with worth bear a different burden: silence, aggression turned inward or outward, and little vocabulary for distress. Patriarchy shapes the psychological lives of every gender. Stigma compounds this. Mental illness is still widely seen as a moral failing, a spiritual affliction, a source of family shame. Public awareness of what depression, anxiety, psychosis, or trauma actually involves — and that they are treatable — is limited. People wait for years before seeking care, often turning first to faith healers, informal practitioners, or no one at all. Many of us carry a sense of heaviness at how slowly some things change. It is worth naming that feeling rather than suppressing it. Despair can be worked through collectively. On this World Mental Health Day and beyond, people with lived experience must be heard. Against this backdrop, the launch of the national mental health policy on Oct 1 was a necessary step. A policy places mental health on the public agenda, gives advocates a reference point, and offers the system a direction. The political will behind it must be acknowledged. A launch, however, is a moment, whereas implementation is the work of a decade. Pakistan has over 250 million people. By most estimates, it has roughly 500 psychiatrists and a comparable number of psychologists, with no licensing body to regulate the practice of psychology, and, therefore, no uniform standard of training, scope, or accountability. The scarcity is sharper still in specialist areas. There are fewer than 10 child and adolescent psychiatrists in the country, and child psychologists are almost non-existent. Mental health has been under-resourced for decades. This is not a criticism of any individual or institution. It is the arithmetic of a neglected field, with far-reaching consequences. Where specialists are scarce, implementation tends to fall on others: dedicated NGOs, short-course trainees, and well-intentioned professionals who have not had the opportunity to work with many patients over many years, often without regular supervision. Nuanced, effective mental healthcare rests on the clinical judgement to distinguish grief from depression, trauma from defiance, and a cry for help from a pattern of behaviour that signals something more. That judgement is built through years of practice, mentorship, error corrected under guidance, and slow accumulation of patients’ stories. Without it, even well-designed programmes can overlook those most in need. The need for distinction is greater still given the context. Pakistan contends with floods and heatwaves, economic precarity, displacement, gender-based violence, and the effects of regional conflict — among the principal determinants of mental health. Implementation in such conditions requires people who understand both the science and the street. As we welcome the policy, and look forward to its implementation, some principles deserve consideration. Implementation is best guided by practitioners with long front-line clinical and research experience in the country, supported by public health and systems expertise. Second, a rigorous, costed strategic plan is essential. The design must specify which services will be delivered in which districts, by whom, under whose supervision, and measured against what indicators. Aspiration must be translated into sequence and budget. Third, this must be directed by a coalition of experts. Psychiatrists, psychologists, mental health researchers, paediatricians, educators, social workers, legal experts, and people with lived experience should work at one table rather than in silos. Fourth, funding must match the stated priority. Whether through government allocation or philanthropy, sustained investment in training, supervision, public awareness, and a licensing framework for psychologists is what converts intention into infrastructure. Expanding the specialist pipeline, from child and adolescent services to adult care, would be transformative. International expertise is valuable, and Pakistan will continue to benefit from shared learning. Yet the durability of any approach depends on its fit with local realities: the district hospital, the crowded clinic, the family weighing in insistent on joint management and care, the need for task shifting, etc. Those who practise here, and who remain once project cycles end, understand that terrain best. If this year’s theme is to be taken seriously, clinicians and communities on the ground belong at the centre of this work and at the helm of it, not at its margins. Above all, people with lived experience must be heard. The woman who wants to study, the boy who wants permission to feel, and the adult who has suffered silently for years are telling us what they need: safety, dignity, and to be believed. No policy will succeed if it is written about them rather than with them. On this World Mental Health Day, we might resolve to build a system as thoughtful as the people it is meant to serve. The policy is a promise. Keeping it will require patience, expertise, and humility. The writer is a consultant child, adolescent and adult psychiatrist and founder & CEO at Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute.Instagram:@lookslikeapsychiatrist

articles.title: Pakistan’s Yemen moment
articles.content: ON Oct 5, in an emergency meeting, the member states of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreementinvokedthe joint defence clause. Now, Islamabad and Ankara can actively move towards rapid force deployment to protect Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. The Middle East is one of the most complex and conflict-prone regions. The decision to operationalise the collective defence clause in less than two months of signing the MJDA suggests that Islamabad might remain embroiled in several layers of Middle Eastern conflicts in future under these security commitments. This is a classic Pakistan-Yemen moment, which the previous PML-N government avoided in 2015. Saudi Arabia officially asked Pakistan in 2015 to join its coalition against Yemen’s Houthis. However, Pakistan chose to remain neutral. More than a decade after Pakistan took one of its toughest foreign policy decisions, the Yemen moment has resurfaced. This time, however, Pakistan has made security commitments to Saudi Arabia under the MJDA in 2026 and theStrategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed last year. Yemen is one of the most complex cases of civil unrest and conflict, illustrating how external actors can complicate regional and domestic conflict dynamics. Following a Saudi-led coalition’s seven-year intervention from 2015 to 2022, the UN brokered a truce. However, a final peace agreement remains pending. Consequently, until a formal Saudi-Houthi accord is finalised, Pakistan alongside Ankara may face prolonged military deployments lasting months or even years to bolster Saudi defence forces within their territory. Despite these operational challenges, Pakistan must fulfil its security commitments to Saudi Arabia. In the realm of global geopolitics, a nation’s security commitments are the bedrock of its external power projection and diplomatic leverage. Having formally elevated its bilateral arrangements into the binding, Nato-like collective security framework of the MJDA, Islamabad cannot afford to hesitate when the pact is invoked. Therefore, Pakistan must fulfil its security obligations wholeheartedly to safeguard its strategic credibility. Furthermore, the economic dimension of this relationship underpins Pakistan’s very survival. Saudi Arabia has historically stood as Islamabad’s premier economic anchor during its darkest balance-of-payments and liquidity crises. To survive a perilous geopolitical tightrope, Pakistan must immediately execute a sophisticated, active, and dual-front diplomatic strategy. While Islamabad must deliver on its collective defence commitment to Saudi Arabia, it cannot afford a catastrophic fallout with its western neighbour, Iran. Pakistan shares a volatile, 900-kilometre border with Iran, a frontier already plagued by cross-border militancy and fragile security dynamics. Direct military entanglement with the Iranian ‘Axis of Resistance’, or an operational misstep that Tehran perceives as hostile, would trigger an asymmetric blowback along the Balochistan border, destabilise Pakistan’s internal security, and ruin vital regional trade prospects. To survive this perilous geopolitical tightrope, Pakistan must immediately execute a sophisticated, active, and dual-front diplomatic strategy. The first pillar of this strategy requires active diplomatic engagement with Iran to negotiate a comprehensive, long-term peace treaty between Riyadh and Tehran. By signing or even negotiating a peace treaty between the two capitals, Islamabad will likely be able to reduce regional tensions and minimise concerns of direct military confrontation under the MJDA with Iran. Islamabad is uniquely positioned for this role. Recently, Islamabad garnered significant diplomatic goodwill by acting as a trusted backchannel and mediator between the US and Iran.Islamabad’s mediatory role brought the US and Irandirectly to the negotiating table, which culminated in the Islamabad MoU. However, given the immense scale of the current regional mistrust, hostilities, and crisis, Pakistan cannot walk this path alone. To maximise the probability of success, Islamabad must integrate China into a co-mediatory process. This joint Beijing-Islamabad peace initiative can offer the perfect synergy of regional solutions for regional tensions. China has been viewed as a factor of stability in South Asia and the Middle East. While Pakistan possesses deep, institutionalised defence ties with Riyadh, and a shared diplomatic vocabulary with Tehran, China enjoys immense economic influence over both nations through its Belt and Road Initiative, and comprehensive strategic partnership agreement with Iran. Beijing has already demonstrated its diplomatic capability by successfully brokering the historic Saudi-Iran normalisation pact in 2023. By combining Islamabad’s strategic clout with China’s economic heft, this collaborative framework can offer Riyadh and Tehran structural security guarantees and economic incentives, respectively. These two elements can transform a fragile status quo into a durable, written peace treaty. The second, equally critical pillar of Pakistan’s diplomatic strategy demands the immediate establishment of robust, direct, and uninterrupted communication channels between Islamabad and Tehran. As the MJDA moves from a paper agreement to rapid, physical deployment on the ground, the risk of miscalculation and misinterpretation of certain actions escalates exponentially. In a highly securitised environment, defensive posturing can easily be misconstrued as preparation for an offensive strike. Pakistan must institutionalise a permanent, high-level military-to-military and intelligence-sharing hotline with Iran. This will help Islamabad and Tehran curb disinformation campaigns by adversarial third parties or non-state actors that want to drive a wedge between Pakistan and Iran. For years, Islamabad aspired to balance its relationship between Saudi Arabia and Iran. Perhaps Pakistan’s Yemen moment has arrived to test this balancing approach. Pakistan’s true value to both Riyadh and the broader Gulf region lies in its unique capacity to act as a credible, neutral mediator between the GCC and Iran. Pakistan cannot afford to back off from its defence commitments to Riyadh, but equally, it cannot afford to strain its ties with Tehran. Therefore, Islamabad’s Yemen moment should not damage its credibility as a defence partner of Saudi Arabia, nor create rifts with its important neighbour, Iran. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.X:@itskhurramabbas
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: Eliminating the past
articles.content: IT was the demolition of a mosque that catapulted the Bharatiya Janata Party into political prominence. The Vishwa Hindu Parishad began the campaign to destroy Babri Masjid in the 1980s. The BJP was its political voice. In December 1992, the mosque was demolished, and the pretence was that the destruction was driven by an angry mob. The inquiry commission looking into the matter found that the destruction was planned. Senior BJP leaders, including the then Uttar Pradesh chief minister Kalyan Singh, were implicated. Nothing happened to the culprits, and by 2019, when the BJP was entrenched in power, India’s apex court handed over the Ayodhya site to the Hindu parties for the construction of the Ram Temple. The BJP has clung to mosque-related disputes as a political strategy through the decades, and the statistics are truly alarming. A recent report by the Millat Times, an Indian Muslim publication, found at least 2,126 instances of demolition, removal and eviction involving mosques and other Muslim sites, including madressahs and dargahs, since 2020. Most of the demolitions have been in Uttar Pradesh — home to millions of Indian Muslims, and hence a target for the BJP. Last month, it was the turn of the Saharanpur mosque, which stood inside the district administration complex in Uttar Pradesh. In the early morning of Sept 5, 2026, excavators and bulldozers were used to raze it. There would no longer be any prayers there. The city magistrate and sub-divisional magistrate were present, alongside police and paramilitary forces. Lok Sabha MP Iqra Hasan was placed under effective house arrest to prevent her from protesting against the demolition of the century-old mosque. The story of how the Saharanpur mosque was demolished, and how institutions, including courts, failed to protect it, can be read as the general destruction of protections for minorities in India. It began in 2025, when a complaint alleged that the mosque had been illegally built on government land. The mosque, which had existed for over 115 years in the same spot, was suddenly considered an illegal structure. The mosque issue is central to what is taking place in India today. By July 2026, the 315-square-metre complex had been declared an “unauthorised occupation” and ordered vacated. Last month, a district judge dismissed the mosque committee’s appeal. The mosque’s representatives filed a petition with the Allahabad High Court, alleging that no legal notice was provided for the demolition. The writ petition is still with the court. The story of the Saharanpur demolition is similar to many other instances of desecration of religious sites. The hatred towards Muslims and the destruction of Islamic heritage is central to the BJP programme. Regular demolitions, framed as Hindu religious mobilisation or yatras, are now a mainstay of Indian politics. It is not just the Millat Times that has been trying to draw attention to these demolitions. Amnesty International’s 2024 report on “bulldozer injustice” in India noted that in 75 cases, only six were given prior notice. Amnesty viewed the forced evictions and consequent demolitions as violations of international law. Pakistan should take note of the last bit. It is essential for Pakistan to distinguish itself from India by giving proper protection to its own religious minorities so that it can demonstrate its belief in minority rights. And it must raise the mosque demolition issue internationally. That a once shining example of democracy now looks away when hundreds of years of its history are wiped out by the BJP’s eager bulldozers is aston-ishing. The mosque issue is central to what is taking place in India today. The ease with which local officials give sanction to the rabid Islamophobia of the BJP’s army of bhakts reveals the hollowing out of Indian democracy. The current protests over the tampering of voter rolls are just another chapter in this story. In deciding what is or is not official, the BJP has declared everything — from mosques and voters to everyone it believes antithetical to Hindu supremacy — to be illegal. Hindutva’s conception of religious majoritarianism is a curse upon Indian minorities. The destruction of thousands of mosques is evidence of how it has played out: erasing and razing everything and everyone that does not accord with its dangerous worldview centred on Hindu ‘supremacy’. It is an open question whether the current protests in India will be able to truly contest the brainwashing of an entire nation. In the meantime, the only certainty is that tomorrow the BJP will target yet another mosque and plan yet another demolition. The writer is an attorney teachingconstitutional law and political philosophy.rafia.zakaria@gmail.com

articles.title: Legal remedies
articles.content: THE missing persons’ issue is not new. The post-Soviet political tumult in the world released the pent-up energy of ethnic and ideological conflicts that had lain dormant under the stabilising hold of totalitarianism. Consequently, as armed conflicts amongst and within nations intensified, the number of missing persons remained high during the mid-1990s. An international commission for missing persons was established in 1996 to track and resolve the issue in Yugoslavia’s conflict. The commission’s mandate was expanded in 2003 to include the global issues of missing persons in various conflicts, natural disasters, and climate migrations. The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance was signed in 2006, which defined enforced disappearance as “the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the state or by persons or groups of persons acting with the authorisation, support or acquiescence of the state”. The treaty entered into force in 2010. The missing persons issue got further traction with the rise of ideologically inspired waves of terrorism by organisations like Al Qaeda, IS and several others. UNSC resolutions 1267, 1998, and 2253 established a list of terrorist entities including Al Qaeda, the Taliban, and IS to sanction these along with their financiers. Despite these international efforts, the domestic legal options to deal with terrorist entities remained fragmented. As a consequence, the issue of missing persons was conflated with the issue of enforced disappearances. Our low terrorism prosecution rate signals dysfunction. It is difficult to separate voluntary and enforced disappearances globally. In Pakistan, a Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances was established in 2011 which has dealt with 10,947 missing persons’ cases throughout Pakistan and has resolved 9,447 (86 per cent) cases. When judicial prosecution of hardened criminals becomes ineffective, it can create incentives for law-enforcement agencies to resort to vigilante justice. This can further create space for allegations of enforced disappearances where apprehension of terrorism suspects is not immediately followed by prosecution. Due care needs to be taken to sift cases of voluntary disappearances, crime-related arrests, and terrorism-related detentions. Differential legal treatment and prosecution are required to avoid a predilection for non-legal remedies on the part of LEAs. Pakistan’s low terrorism prosecution rate (8pc) over the past two decades, compared with 88pc in the UK, 99pc in China and 99.9pc in Japan, signals a dysfunctional prosecution system. The inordinate delays in prosecution and conviction of terrorists create space for their political supporters to exploit legal gaps and build victimhood narratives. In Balochistan, terrorist organisations have spawned a fear psychosis by abducting judges in order to stymie the prosecution process. A few examples include the assassination of justice Muhammad Noor Meskanzai, former chief justice of Balochistan High Court in Kharan in 2022, and killing of district and sessions judge Abdul Hakeem Kaka in Mastung in July 2026. The threat extends beyond judges, with around 50 CTD officials killed in Balochistan, while the driver of a law officer was shot when the officer was recording his statement concerning the July 2026 Ziarat terrorist attack in which 27 policemen were killed. To tackle these challenges, the government has amended Pakistan’s Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) 1997 through the insertion of Section 11-EEEE that provides for ‘Preventive Detention for Inquiry’, allowing detention for up to 90 days for inquiry, thereby providing a legal mechanism for investigating terrorism suspects by collecting evidence before moving to prosecute them. The Anti-Terrorism (Balochistan Amendment) Act, 2025, incorporates the amended ATA, 1997, to the province, enabling LEAs and the judiciary to detain the accused for 90 days, while Section 21-AAA of the Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Act, 2026, provides protection to judges and witnesses. Since the implementation of the new law in Balochistan, out of 90 detainees, five have been released where the allegations could not be established, while 40 have been referred for trial through faceless courts, demonstrating movement from preventive detention towards prosecution through a defined legal process. All the above measures show the government’s resolve to extend the full range of legal remedies to LEAs and the judiciary to arrest, investigate, and prosecute the terrorists, with celerity, and in accordance with the law, bringing much-needed transparency and fairness to the whole process. The writer has a PhD from Nust.rwjanj@hotmail.com

articles.title: A voice in care
articles.content: WORLD Mental Health Day this year carries a compelling message. The theme, ‘Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change’, challenges a practice in which patients are passive recipients of care rather than people whose experiences can improve it. The message is particularly relevant to Pakistan, which launched its National Mental Health Policy 2026-2035 earlier this month. The policy promises to bring treatment closer to communities, an encouraging development in a country where some 32.4m people need mental healthcare and access to services remains desperately limited. However, expanding treatment is only part of the challenge. Patients must also have a voice in determining what kind of care they receive, how they are treated, and whether services meet their needs. Otherwise, even well-intentioned reforms risk overlooking the people they are supposed to help. A Pakistani woman’s experience, highlighted by the WHO this week, illustrates why this matters. Sania suffered depression as a teenager but later came to understand how social circumstances could shape psychological distress. She questioned whether problems rooted in discrimination, insecurity and restricted freedoms could be addressed through medical treatment alone. Her subsequent work helped bring the views of people with mental health conditions into discussions surrounding Pakistan’s new policy. Her experience raises an important question: what happens when a woman suffering from anxiety lives in an abusive household, or a young man battling depression cannot find work? Medication and counselling may be necessary, but they cannot remove the pressures contributing to their distress. For poorer households, even travelling to a distant clinic can mean losing a day’s wages. In Pakistan, where families often make decisions on behalf of vulnerable loved ones and mental illness carries shame, protecting patients’ right to make choices about their care is particularly important. The recently concluded Islamabad mental health summit promised greater community participation and closer monitoring of improvements to mental healthcare. Those commitments now require action. Provincial governments should ensure that people who have experienced mental illness, along with caregivers, are represented in bodies overseeing mental health services. Hospitals must strengthen safeguards for informed consent, create confidential channels for complaints, and protect patients against degrading or coercive treatment. The authorities should also publish figures on patient complaints and how they are resolved. Community-based care should allow people to remain connected to their families, education and livelihoods wherever clinically appropriate. Equally important, patients must be involved in evaluating whether these services actually work. Pakistan has spent years discussing the stigma surrounding mental illness. This World Mental Health Day, it should begin listening to those who know the system’s flaws first-hand.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Midterm break
articles.content: AMERICAN President Donald Trump’sstatementthat he will not launch a fresh attack on Iran before the US midterm elections does little to calm fears of renewed war in the Gulf. In effect, the US president has only promised to postpone the attack, when he should have committed to indefinitely suspending hostilities in favour of dialogue. Clearly, it is a calculated political move: the Iran war is unpopular with the American people, mainly because of the inflation and high petroleum prices it has caused. Mr Trump may be holding off on a new assault to prevent a complete drubbing of the Republicans at the ballot box. What is perplexing is the mixed messaging. While refusing to rule out a post-midterms attack, he also said that the Iran war was going toend “very soon”. Most observers have lost count of how many times he has said this. He added that talks with Tehran were “productive”. Should the world believe that a new attack is imminent after the US elections? Or is the US looking to wind things down? Perhaps those calling the shots in Washington themselves do not know. It is also a matter of concern that Israel is reportedly contemplating another attack on Iran. Both the US and Israel need to halt their destructive misadventures in the Middle East. Their irresponsible warmongering has resulted in widespread bloodshed across the region and has upended the global economy. Washington and Tehran have exchanged proposals on how to end the conflict. Mr Trump and his cohorts, therefore, need to concentrate exclusively on the diplomatic track, instead of fuelling speculation regarding fresh hostilities. Already, theYemen conflictis spiralling out of control. If the US and Israel were to spark another round of violence with Iran, the consequences for the entire region — indeed the world at large — would be grim. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is already constrained. If Bab al-Mandeb were also to be closed, and the export of petrochemicals from the region curtailed further because of conflict, the entire world will pay the price for the deadly follies of Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Therefore, instead of speaking in riddles, President Trump must commit his country to the peace process, offer the Iranians a fair deal, and bring his military home from the Middle East.
articles.author: Editorial
